Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for data residency and throughput. Key concerns: long-context support (32k/64k), multilingual quality (Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi), tool-calling to internal ticketing systems, and SOC2/KMS for logs. transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-09 15:30 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Luis Moreno (Polyglot CTO), Anika Rao (Lead ML Engineer), Daniel Kim (DevOps), Priya Shah (PM)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Ethan is our systems SE. Luis: thanks for having us. Could we do quick intros?

[00:10] Luis Moreno: Sure — Luis, CTO, Polyglot Consulting. We build multi-lingual customer automation for enterprise telco and finance customers. Anika: hi, Lead ML, working on prompt design and model eval. Daniel: infra, mostly on VPC and on-prem. Priya: product.

[00:30] Ethan Park: Great. Today the ask is model fit and deployment options — whether Hosted API, Redwood Dedicated, or Redwood Private. We'll also cover context length needs, multilingual performance, and tool-calling. Sound right?

[00:40] Priya Shah: Yep, especially tool-calling — we need the assistant to open tickets, redact PII, and call our billing API.

[01:05] Anika Rao: Also context: we need to ingest long chat histories and CRM docs, sometimes >40k tokens. So long context support is important.

[01:25] Ethan Park: Understood. Quick architecture question: are you planning to do retrieval-augmented generation with a vector DB, or append full transcripts into the prompt?

[01:40] Luis Moreno: Mix of both. For fast replies we use RAG. But for escalations we sometimes want whole conversation context to do summarization and for audit.

[02:00] Maya Chen: Okay — rough clarification on scale: how many requests per second and concurrency?

[02:10] Daniel Kim: Peak is about 35 concurrent sessions, average 1500 requests per hour, but spikes during morning by 3x. Latency target sub-600ms for short queries, longer for batch summarization.

[02:35] Ethan Park: That helps. For model choices, are you leaning open models or closed like OpenAI?

[02:45] Luis Moreno: We prefer open models to avoid vendor lock-in and to run in our VPC for regulated clients. Cost is a factor too.

[03:05] Anika Rao: For language coverage, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Hindi, and some Arabic. Also low-resource dialects.

[03:20] Ethan Park: Good. For open models, two axes matter: base capability (multilingual and instruction following) and long-context support. Models folks commonly mention are Llama 3 variants, Mistral, Mistral x-large, and other community forks. We also sometimes use Llama variants with quantization. Note: folks sometimes call Llama 'Lama' in notes, so apologies if transcription.

[03:55] Luis Moreno: Right. How does Redwood handle large context lengths? We heard about KV cache and prefix caching.

[04:10] Ethan Park: Exactly — our runtime supports sequence lengths up to 64k depending on model and quant profile. We manage KV cache to avoid recomputing context for streaming generations, and prefix caching to store frequently used system prompts. There are tradeoffs: longer context increases memory and latency per request and affects batching efficiency.

[04:45] Daniel Kim: So for 64k sessions, does that mean I need nodes with more GPU memory or do you shard?

[04:55] Ethan Park: For 64k you typically need more memory; we use model parallelism/sharding in Dedicated and Private modes. For Hosted we offer certain verified model variants with 64k support; it depends on the exact model and quantization (8-bit is common, 4-bit can be done but with caveats).

[05:20] Priya Shah: What about multilingual quality — do we need fine-tuning? We want to avoid heavy fine-tuning due to cost.

[05:30] Anika Rao: In our experiments, base models do ok on Spanish and Portuguese but struggle on Hindi and some Arabic dialects. We wondered if Redwood recommends instruction-tuning, LoRA, or retrieval augmentation.

[05:50] Ethan Park: Retrieval is often the lowest-cost win; feeding in better context, curated examples, and using lightweight LoRA adapters for domain-specific terminology usually helps. We recommend evals across languages; we can run those for you.

[06:10] Maya Chen: We should talk deployment choices: Hosted gives fastest time to market; Dedicated gives reserved capacity and predictable latency; Private (VPC/on-prem) addresses data residency and control. Which is most relevant for Polyglot?

[06:30] Luis Moreno: For most customers, Dedicated will be fine but our top enterprise clients require VPC with no logs leaving their network — so Private might be necessary. Also KMS requirements for key management.

[06:55] Ethan Park: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations and can run in air-gapped environments. For audit logs, we can stream logs to your SIEM and provide retention options. For the Dedicated offering we maintain SOC2 compliance and can provide attestations.

[07:25] Daniel Kim: About tool-calling: we need secure tool integrations that can redact PII before tool invocation. Does Redwood provide a tool sandbox or do we manage that?

[07:40] Ethan Park: Our platform supports structured tool calling — you can define tool schemas and the runtime enforces argument types. For PII redaction we recommend a pre-invocation hook: the request passes through a lightweight filter (could be your code or ours) that redacts or tokens that need gating. We also support a policy layer for data exfiltration prevention.

[08:15] Anika Rao: Is function calling identical across Hosted/Dedicated/Private? Will the same API work?

[08:25] Maya Chen: Yes — same API surface. Tool manifests and function schemas are portable. For Private you manage the actual tool endpoints; for Hosted we can host connectors but with enterprise agreements.

[08:45] Luis Moreno: Any notable model-specific gotchas — e.g., Mistral being weaker in Hindi, or Llama requiring particular tokenizers?

[08:55] Ethan Park: Tokenization differences do matter; some models use sentencepiece variants that tokenize non-latin text differently. We do per-model multilingual benchmarks. For instance, some Mistral forks have stronger English performance but lag on Hindi out of the box. Llama 3 multi-lingual variants with instruction-tuning perform well, but licensing/weights vary and we'd confirm.

[09:30] Maya Chen: Cost questions — what's the unit economics between Hosted and Dedicated per million tokens?

[09:40] Maya Chen: (AE note: provided rough examples on call) Hosted tends to be higher per-token but includes management and autoscaling. Dedicated lowers per-token compute cost but requires a commit and reserve. We'll share a comparison table.

[10:05] Priya Shah: For benchmarks, can you run our prompt set across 8k, 32k and 64k contexts with our top-12 languages? We want latency and quality scores, and a cost estimate.

[10:20] Ethan Park: Yes — we'll run the RAG pipelines and full context summarization. For 64k full-context summarization we may need Private or larger Dedicated nodes to match latency targets. We'll surface per-request memory and GPU usage.

[10:45] Luis Moreno: Security: do you preserve transcripts in Hosted? We have clients that will not allow transcript retention.

[10:55] Ethan Park: For Hosted we have retention controls and can disable storage; there are tradeoffs for logging and debugging. Dedicated/Private gives you full control — Private can be set to never persist transcripts outside customer-owned storage. We support customer-managed encryption keys.

[11:20] Anika Rao: Any suggestions on model distillation/quantization to lower costs while keeping multilingual quality?

[11:30] Ethan Park: 8-bit quant gives good cost/quality sweet spot. 4-bit can be done but requires careful evaluation — some languages show degradation. We also do kernel selection and compilation per model to get better throughput. For critical languages we recommend mixed strategy: larger model for hard languages, smaller cheaper variant for common queries. Smart routing can handle that.

[12:05] Maya Chen: Let's recap next steps. Ethan will run benchmarks across 8k/32k/64k on sample prompts and languages. Maya will share Dedicated pricing and Private architecture docs plus SOC2. Luis will share prompt set and compliance checklist.

[12:30] Luis Moreno: Sounds good. Also want to include a short pilot — maybe a 6-week pilot on Dedicated with a 32k config for a couple of tier-1 clients.

[12:45] Maya Chen: We can draft a pilot scope and success criteria: latency under 600ms for short queries, F1/ROUGE thresholds for summarization in Spanish/Hindi, and secure tool-calling with PII redaction.

[13:05] Priya Shah: Who is the technical contact for the benchmark?

[13:10] Ethan Park: That would be me — I'll coordinate.

[13:20] Daniel Kim: From infra side we'll need a network diagram and any inbound/outbound ports if we look at Private.

[13:30] Maya Chen: We'll include a standard Private network diagram and a list of endpoints.

[13:45] Luis Moreno: Any gotchas on model licensing when moving from Hosted to Private?

[13:55] Ethan Park: Some open weights have license terms restricting commercial use; we vet each model. For enterprise we often recommend certified model bundles that avoid ambiguous licenses. We'll include that in the model selection doc.

[14:10] Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deliverables and schedule the on-prem feasibility call.

[14:20] (end)

Notes about transcript: occasional mis-transcriptions: 'Llama' noted as 'Lama' in a couple spots; 'Mistral' once transcribed as 'Mistrial'. Speaker overlaps and filler words preserved.
